items.title: 6.11.1 Entropy, diffusion and the number of ways of arrangement

blocks.text: Molecules in a vapour diffuse by chance, which can be shown by thinking about the probability of finding them in one place at any one time. In the simplified model of Figure 6.10, three molecules in gas jar A are separated from an empty gas jar B by a partition; when it is opened there are eight different ways for the molecules to arrange themselves in the two jars: the number of molecules in A is 3, the number of jars 2, and the number of possible arrangements is 2^3 = 8. With five molecules there would be 2^5 = 32 ways, and with a hundred 2^100. In general the number of ways is x^y, where x is the number of places and y the number of particles. Diffusion happens because there is a very large number of ways of arranging the molecules; the concept of the number of ways of arranging particles, or the energy within them, helps predict whether a change can happen.

blocks.alt: Top left: two jars with a red partition, three numbered molecules in the left jar, and the counting of arrangements below. Lower left: entropy comparisons by state, number of particles and hardness, and the calcium oxide entropy calculation. Right: boxes with H = G + TS and delta G = delta H - T delta S, the Haber process and calcium sulfate examples, and a table of the sign of delta G from the signs of delta H and delta S.
blocks.caption: Entropy as the number of ways of arrangement, entropy comparisons, and Gibbs free energy (original diagram after Figure 6.10 and the printed examples of topics 6.11 and 6.12).
blocks.long_description: Each of the three molecules can be in either jar once the partition opens, giving 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 arrangements, and a hundred molecules give 2^100: diffusion wins because the spread-out arrangements vastly outnumber the gathered ones. Entropy rises from solid to liquid to gas, with more particles, and with softer structures. The free energy delta G = delta H - T delta S is negative for a spontaneous change: the Haber process at 25 degrees C gives -33.1 kJ, the dissolving of calcium sulfate +25.3 kJ.

blocks.prompt: 100 molecules of a gas are in jar A, connected to an evacuated jar B. When the stopcock is opened, how many arrangements are possible, and why does the gas never return to jar A by itself?
blocks.explanation: 2^100 arrangements, because each molecule may be in either of the two jars. Only one of these arrangements has all hundred molecules back in A, so the chance of the gas gathering there again is negligibly small; the many spread-out arrangements make diffusion effectively irreversible.

items: Number of ways = x^y (x places, y particles): 3 molecules in 2 jars give 2^3 = 8, 5 give 32, 100 give 2^100; diffusion happens because spread-out arrangements are overwhelmingly more numerous.
